record.paper_title: Finiteness and periodicity of beta expansions – number theoretical and dynamical open problems
record.original_question: In the two-dimensional shift radix system parameter plane with coordinates (x,y), prove or disprove that every point in the region {(x,y) | 0 < 2x < y < x + 1} defines a shift radix system; equivalently, determine whether that whole open region is an SRS region.

evidence.quote: Problem 8. Prove (or disprove) that {(x, y) | 0 < 2x < y < x + 1} is a SRS region.
The essential difficulty of this problem exists around (1, 2).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a parameter vector $r=(r_0,r_1,\dots,r_{d-1})\in\mathbb{R}^d$, define the mapping $\tau_r:\mathbb{Z}^d\to\mathbb{Z}^d$ by
$$\tau_r(a_0,a_1,\dots,a_{d-1}) = (a_1,a_2,\dots,a_{d-1},-\lfloor r_0 a_0 + r_1 a_1 + \cdots + r_{d-1}a_{d-1}\rfloor).$$
The parameter $r$ is called a shift radix system (SRS) if for every $a\in\mathbb{Z}^d$ there exists $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $\tau_r^n(a)=0$. Let
$$\mathcal{D}_d := \{r\in\mathbb{R}^d : r \text{ is an SRS}\}.$$
Consider the two-dimensional case $d=2$ with parameters $(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2$, where
$$\tau_{(x,y)}(a_0,a_1) = (a_1, -\lfloor x a_0 + y a_1 \rfloor).$$
Prove or disprove that
$$\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2 : 0 < 2x < y < x+1\} \subseteq \mathcal{D}_2,$$
i.e., that every point of this open region defines a shift radix system.
artifact.status_search_result: The characterization of the SRS region $\mathcal{D}_2$ in two dimensions is acknowledged in surveys on shift radix systems as a hard, still-unresolved problem; the precise sub-region $\{0<2x<y<x+1\}$ appears among open problems and no proof or disproof of full SRS-membership for this triangular region has been located.

status_evidence.title: Shift Radix Systems - A Survey
status_evidence.snippet: Characterization of all r in R^d which give rise to an SRS is a hard problem; a complete solution seems out of range, especially in dimension 2 and higher.
status_evidence.claim: The full characterization of the 2D SRS region remains open.
